siva_et:
1.1 Dhritarashtra said  What did my people and the sons of Pandu do when they had assembled
together eager for battle on the holy plain of Kurukshetra, O Sanjaya.
summary: Sitting in the dark, a blind king anxiously asks what is happening on the battlefield of life where opposing forces have gathered.

siva_et:
1.2. Sanjaya said  Having seen the army of the Pandavas drawn up in battle-array,
King Duryodhana then approached his teacher (Drona) and spoke these words.
summary: Faced with an intimidating opposing force, a leader anxiously sizes up the competition and rushes to strategize.

siva_et:
1.3. "Behold, O Teacher! this mighty army of the sons of Pandu,
arrayed by the son of Drupada, thy wise disciple.
summary: Looking at the strength of those opposing you can spark sudden feelings of intimidation and doubt.

siva_et:
1.4. Here are heroes, mighty archers, eal in battle to Bhima
and Arjuna, Yoyudhana (Satyaki), Virata and Drupada, of the great car (mighty
warriors).
summary: It is easy to become overwhelmed when you start counting the skills and strengths of the people standing against you.

siva_et:
1.5. "Dhrishtaketu, chekitana and the valiant king of Kasi, Purujit
and Kuntibhoja and Saibya, the best men.
summary: A nervous inventory of opposing forces reveals a formidable line-up of challengers ready to face you.

siva_et:
1.6. "The strong Yodhamanyu and the brave Uttamaujas, the son
of Subhadra (Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadra and Arjuna), and the sons of
Draupadi, all of great chariots (great heroes).
summary: The sheer number of capable opponents can make the mountain you have to climb feel even steeper.
In moments of high tension, taking stock of who is on your side helps steady your nerves for the challenge ahead.

siva_et:
1.8. "Thyself and Bhishma, and Karna and also Kripa, the victorious
in war, Asvatthama, Vikarna, and also Bhurisrava, the son of Somadatta.
summary: You reflect on the fierce loyalties and trusted allies you have gathered in your corner to face the conflict.

siva_et:
1.9. "And also many other heroes who are ready to give up their
lives for my sake, armed with various weapons and missiles, all well-skilled
in battle.
summary: There are people in your life who care so deeply for you that they are ready to lay down everything to support your cause.

siva_et:
1.10. "This army of ours marshalled by Bhishma is insufficient,
whereas that army of theirs marshelled by Bhima is sufficient.
summary: Self-doubt creeps in as you secretly worry that your own resources fall short compared to the opposition.

siva_et:
1.11. "Therefore do ye all, stationed in your respective positions,
in the several divisions of the army, protect Bhishma alone."
summary: A call to stand firm in your assigned place and protect your core strengths when pressure mounts.

siva_et:
1.12. His glorious grandsire (Bhishma), the oldest of the Kauravas,
in order to cheer Duryodhana, now roared like a lion, and blew his conch.
summary: A seasoned elder lets out a powerful roar of confidence to shake off your fears and boost your courage.

siva_et:
1.13. Then (following Bhishma), conches and kettledrums, tabors,
drums and cow horns blared forth ite suddenly (from the Kaurava side)
and the sound was tremendous.
summary: A sudden, thunderous clash of instruments shatters the silence, signaling that the confrontation has officially begun.

siva_et:
1.14. Then, also, Madhava (Krishna) and the son of Pandu (Arjuna),
seated in the magnificent chariot, yoked with white horses, blew divine
conches.
summary: Amidst the rising chaos, divine allies blow their conches to remind you that you are not facing your battles alone.

siva_et:
1.15. Hrishikesha blew the Panchajanya and Arjuna blew the Devadatta
and Bhima (the wolf-bellied), the doer of terrible deeds, blew the great
conch Paundra.
summary: The heroes blow their powerful conch shells, signaling readiness to stand and face what lies ahead with courage.

siva_et:
1.16. The king Yodhishthira, the son of Kunti, blew the Anantavijaya;
Nakula and Sahadeva blew the Sughosha and the Manipushpaka.
summary: Each leader sounds their unique conch, ready to take responsibility and step into the challenges of the moment.

siva_et:
1.17. The king of Kasi, an exellent archer, Sikhandi, the mighty
car-warrior, Dhrishtadyumna and Virata and Satyaki, the unconered.
summary: Mighty warriors and skilled archers prepare for the impending trial, showing steadfast resolve in the face of conflict.

siva_et:
1.18. Drupada and the sons of Draupadi, O Lord of the earth, and
the son of Subhadra, the mighty-armed, blew their conches separately.
summary: The great defenders of the land raise their voices and horns together, committing fully to the path they must walk.

siva_et:
1.19. That tumultuous sound rent the hearts of (the members of)
Dhritarashtra's party, making both the heaven and the earth resound.
summary: A sudden, booming sound echoes across earth and sky, striking deep anxiety into the hearts of the opposition.

siva_et:
1.20. Then, seeing the people of Dhritarashtra’s party standing
arrayed and the discharge of weapons about to begin, Arjuna, the son of
Pandu, whose ensign was a monkey, took up his bow and said the following
to Krishna, O Lord of the earth.
summary: As the weapons are drawn and the tension peaks, Arjuna steps forward, pausing at the edge of the conflict to take a breath.

siva_et:
1.21 Arjuna said  In the middle between the two armies, place my chariot,
O krishna, so that I may behold those who stand here desirous to fight,
and know with whom I must fight, when the battle is about to commence.
summary: Arjuna asks to pause right in the middle of the chaos so he can truly look at who he is about to face and understand his situation.

siva_et:
1.22. Arjuna said  In the middle between the two armies, place my chariot,
O krishna, so that I may behold those who stand here desirous to fight,
and know with whom I must fight, when the battle is about to commence.
summary: With a desire for clarity, Arjuna seeks a moment of stillness between opposing forces to properly assess what is happening around him.

siva_et:
1.23. For I desire to observe those who are assembled here to fight,
wishing to please in battle the evil-minded Duryodhana (the son of Dhritarashtra).
summary: Arjuna pauses to look closely at those who have gathered, bearing the heavy weight of the conflicting loyalties and relationships before him.

siva_et:
1.24. Sanjaya said  Thus addressed by Arjuna, Krishna, having stationed that
best of chariots, O Dhritarashtra, in the midst of the two armies.
summary: Krishna graciously guides and positions the chariot right where it needs to be, offering steady support in a time of uncertainty.

siva_et:
1.25. In front of Bhishma and Drona, and all the rulers of the
earth, said: "O Arjuna (son of Pritha), behold these Kurus gathered together."
summary: Looking out across the field, Arjuna is invited to witness the assembled family and teachers standing ready for what comes next.

siva_et:
1.26. Then, Arjuna (son of Pritha) saw there (in the armies) stationed,
fathers and grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons
and friends too.
summary: Suddenly, Arjuna recognizes the faces of his beloved family members, teachers, and lifelong friends standing on both sides of the line.

siva_et:
1.27. (He saw) fathers-in-law and friends also in both the armies.
The son of Kunti, Arjuna, seeing all those kinsmen thus standing arrayed,
spoke this, sorrowfully filled with deep pity.
summary: Seeing all his loved ones arrayed against each other, Arjuna is suddenly overcome with a deep wave of sorrow and heartbreak.

siva_et: 1.28. Arjuna said  Seeing these, my kinsmen, O krishna, arrayed, eager to fight.
summary: Overwhelmed by the sight of his own kinsmen gathered for battle, Arjuna's heart breaks at the thought of the pain to come.

siva_et:
1.29. My limbs fail and my mouth is parched, my body ivers and
my hair stands on end.
summary: When hit by overwhelming stress or panic, our bodies can physically shut down, leaving us shaking and depleted.

siva_et:
1.30. The (bow) Gandiva slips from my hand, and also my skins burns
all over; I am unable even to stand and my mind is reeling, as it were.
summary: It is completely normal to feel so anxious and overwhelmed that you lose your focus, drop your tools, and feel entirely unsteady on your feet.

siva_et:
1.31. And I see adverse omens, O Kesava. I do not see any good
in killing my kinsmen in battle.
summary: When faced with painful choices that could hurt the people we care about, our intuition often warns us that nothing good will come of it.

siva_et:
1.32. I desire not victory, O Krishna, nor kingdom, nor pleasures.
Of what avail is dominion to us, O Krishna, or pleasures or even life?
summary: In times of deep emotional pain or moral conflict, external successes and worldly pleasures suddenly lose all their appeal.

siva_et:
1.33. Those for whose sake we desire kingdom, enjoyments and pleasures,
stand here in battle, having renounced life and wealth.
summary: Success and comfort feel hollow when the people we wanted to share them with are no longer by our side.

siva_et:
1.34. Teachers, fathers, sons and also grandfathers, maternal uncles,
fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law and other relatives,-
summary: We are deeply tied to our family networks, mentors, and loved ones, who form the bedrock of our social world.

siva_et:
1.35. These I do not wish to kill, though they kill me, O Krishna,
even for the sake of dominion over the three worlds; leave alone killing
them for the sake of the earth.
summary: Some victories simply cost too much, especially if they require harming the very people we love.

siva_et:
1.36. By killing these sons of Dhritarashtra, what pleasure can
be ours, O Janardana? Only sin will accrue to us from killing these felons.
summary: Hurting others for personal gain only brings inner turmoil and regret in the long run.

siva_et:
1.37. Therefore, we should not kill the sons of Dhritarashtra,
our relatives; for how can we be happy by killing our own people, O Madhava
(Krishna)?
summary: True happiness cannot be built on the suffering and destruction of our own family and friends.

siva_et:
1.38. Though they, with intelligence overpowered by greed, see
no evil in the destruction of families, and no sin in hostility to friends,
summary: When people are blinded by greed or ambition, they often fail to see the damage they are doing to their closest relationships.

siva_et:
1.39. Why should not we who clearly see evil in the destruction
of families, learn to turn away from this sin, O Janardana (Krishna)?
summary: When we clearly recognize the destructive impact of an action, it is our responsibility to step back and choose a better path.

siva_et:
1.40. In the destruction of a family, the immemorial religious
rites of that family perish; on the destruction of spirituality, impiety,
indeed, overcomes the whole family.
summary: When foundational family values and traditions break down, the moral fabric of the home begins to unravel.

siva_et:
1.41. By the prevalence of impiety, O Krishna, the women of
the family become corrupt; and , women being corrupted, O Varshenya (descendant
of Vrishni), there arises intermingling of castes.
summary: A breakdown in shared values and mutual respect within a community can lead to widespread confusion and social decay.

siva_et:
1.42. Confusion of castes leads to hell the slayers of the family,
for their forefathers fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-ball and
water (libations).
summary: Disregarding our deeper cultural and familial responsibilities creates a painful disconnect from our heritage and those who came before us.

siva_et:
1.43. By these evil deeds of the destroyers of the family, which
cause confusion of castes, the eternal religious rites of the caste and
the family are destroyed.
summary: Arjuna worries that breaking family traditions will completely unravel the moral and spiritual foundation of society.

siva_et:
1.44. We have heard, O Janardana, that inevitable is the dwelling
for an unknown period in hell for those men in whose families the religious
practices have been destroyed.
summary: He carries a deep dread that destroying family integrity leads to a lasting, painful spiritual fallout.

siva_et:
1.45. Alas! We are involved in a great sin, in that we are
prepared to kill our kinsmen, through greed for the pleasures of a kingdom.
summary: Arjuna is struck with intense remorse, realizing he is about to slaughter his own flesh and blood simply for worldly power.

siva_et:
1.46. If the sons of Dhritarashtra with weapons in hand should
slay me in battle, unresisting and unarmed, that would be better for me.
summary: He feels so sickened by the thought of violence against loved ones that he'd rather die defenseless than fight back.

siva_et:
1.47. Sanjaya said  Having thus spoken in the midst of the battlefield, Arjuna,
casting away his bow and arrow, sat down on the seat of the chariot with
his mind overwhelmed with sorrow.
summary: Overwhelmed by heartbreak and despair, Arjuna drops his weapons and collapses onto his chariot in utter defeat.

siva_et: 2.1 Sanjaya said  To him who was thus overcome with pity and who was despondent, with eyes full of tears and agitated, Madhusudana (the destroyer of Madhu) or Krishna spoke these words.
summary: As Arjuna sits in tears and deep distress, Krishna steps in to address his overwhelming sorrow.

siva_et: 2.2 The Blessed Lord said  Whence is this perilous strait come upon thee, this dejection which is unworthy of you, disgraceful, and which will close the gates of heaven upon you, O Arjuna?
summary: Krishna gently confronts Arjuna, asking how such unhelpful despair could possibly creep into his mind during a crucial moment.

siva_et: 2.3 Yield not to impotence, O Arjuna, son of Pritha. It does not befit thee. Cast off this mean weakness of the heart! Stand up, O scorcher of the foes!
summary: Urging him to shake off this weak mindset, Krishna tells Arjuna to rise up and step into his true power.

siva_et: 2.4 Arjuna said  How, O Madhusudana, shall I fight in battle with arrows against Bhishma and Drona, who are fit to be worshipped, O destroyer of enemies?
summary: Arjuna questions how he could ever raise a weapon against revered elders and teachers like Bhishma and Drona.

siva_et: 2.5 Better it is, indeed, in this world to accept alms than to slay the most noble teachers. But if I kill them, even in this world all my enjoyments of wealth and fulfilled desires will be stained with (their) blood.
summary: He reasons that begging for scraps is better than enjoying wealth built on the blood of his beloved teachers.

siva_et: 2.6 I can hardly tell which will be better, that we should  coner them or that they should coner us. Even the sons of Dhritarashtra, after slaying whom we do not wish to live, stand facing us.
summary: Trapped in indecision, Arjuna admits he doesn't even know whether winning or losing this war would be worse.

siva_et: 2.7 My heart is overpowered by the taint of pity; my mind is confused as to duty. I ask Thee: Tell me decisively what is good for me. I am Thy disciple. Instruct me who has taken refuge in Thee.
summary: Feeling completely lost and overwhelmed by pity, Arjuna humbles himself and asks Krishna to guide him to what is right.

siva_et: 2.8 I do not see that it would remove this sorrow that burns up my senses, even if I should attain prosperous and unrivalled dominion on earth or lordship over the gods.
summary: Arjuna confesses that even ruling an unmatched empire wouldn't be enough to dry up the burning sorrow inside him.

siva_et: 2.9 Sanjaya said  Having spoken thus to Hrishikesha (the Lord of the senses), Arjuna (the coneror of sleep), the destroyer of foes, said to Krishna, "I will not fight" and became silent.
summary: After baring his soul to Krishna, Arjuna abruptly declares he will not fight and falls into a stubborn silence.

siva_et: 2.10 To him who was despondent in the midst of the two armies, Krishna, as if smiling, O Bharata, spoke these words.
summary: When you are feeling completely overwhelmed and lost between difficult choices, help is close by if you are willing to listen.

siva_et: 2.11 The Blessed Lord said  Thou hast grieved for those that should not be grieved for, yet thou speakest words of wisdom. The wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead.
summary: It is natural to hurt, but true wisdom comes from realizing that life and the soul are far deeper than the temporary losses we mourn.

siva_et: 2.12 Nor at any time indeed was I not, nor thou, nor these rulers of men, nor verily shall we ever cease to be hereafter.
summary: You, your loved ones, and everyone around you have always existed in essence and always will; our true nature is timeless.

siva_et: 2.13 Just as in this body the embodied (soul) passes into childhood, youth and old age, so also does it pass into another body; the firm man does not grieve thereat.
summary: Just as you gracefully transition from childhood to old age, your soul simply moves forward when this body fades, so there is no need to panic.

siva_et: 2.14 The contacts of the senses with the objects, O son of Kunti, which cause heat and cold, pleasure and pain, have a beginning and an end; they are impermanent; endure them bravely, O Arjuna.
summary: Life's highs and lows—heat and cold, joy and pain—come and go like the weather; learn to weather the storms with courage.

siva_et: 2.15 That firm man whom, surely, these afflict not, O chief among men, to whom pleasure and pain are the same, is fit for attaining immortality.
summary: When you stop letting temporary pleasures and pains shake your inner stillness, you open the door to lasting peace.

siva_et: 2.16 The unreal hath no being; there is non-being of the real; the truth about both has been seen by the knowers of the Truth (or the seers of the Essence).
summary: Look past the illusions of the material world to find the unchanging truth that underlies everything.

siva_et: 2.17 Know that to be indestructible, by Which all this is pervaded. None can cause the destruction of That, the Imperishable.
summary: There is a core part of you that is completely indestructible and permeates all of existence—nothing can ever truly destroy it.

siva_et: 2.18 These bodies of the embodied Self, Which is eternal, indestructible and immeasurable, are said to have an end. Therefore fight, O Arjuna.
summary: While physical bodies have an expiration date, the soul within is infinite; knowing this, step up and do what you need to do.

siva_et: 2.19 He who takes the Self to be the slayer and he who thinks It is slain, neither of them ï1knowsï1. It slays not, nor is It slain.
summary: If you think you can truly destroy life, or that your life can be permanently snuffed out, you misunderstand the soul, which cannot kill or be killed.

siva_et: 2.20 It is not born, nor does It ever die; after having been, It again ceases not to be; unborn, eternal, changeless and ancient, It is not killed when the body is killed.
summary: You were never born and you will never truly die; your deepest self is ancient, changeless, and untouched by physical death.

siva_et: 2.21 Whosoever knows It to be indestructible, eternal, unborn and inexhaustible, how can that man slay, O Arjuna, or cause to be slain?
summary: When you truly understand that life is eternal and unbreakable, the heavy burden of fear, guilt, and harm falls away.

siva_et: 2.22 Just as a man casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so also the embodied Self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others which are new.
summary: Death is simply taking off a worn-out set of clothes and putting on new ones, so do not let the change break your heart.

siva_et: 2.23 Weapons cut It not, fire burns It not, water wets It not, wind dries It not.
summary: Your deepest self is entirely invincible—weapons cannot hurt it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot drown it, and wind cannot dry it out.

siva_et: 2.24 This Self cannot be cut, burnt, wetted, nor dried up. It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable and ancient.
summary: Your true essence is completely indestructible and timeless, existing far beyond any physical change or harm.

siva_et: 2.25 This (Self) is said to be unmanifested, unthinkable and unchangeable. Therefore, knowing This to be such, thou shouldst not grieve.
summary: Because your deepest self is beyond human comprehension and change, there is ultimately no reason to let grief consume you.

siva_et: 2.26 But even if thou thinkest of It as being constantly born and constantly dying, even then, O mighty-armed, thou shouldst not grieve.
summary: Even if you look at life as an endless cycle of birth and death, loss is a natural part of the pattern, so you shouldn't despair.

siva_et: 2.27 For certain is death for the born, and certain is birth for the dead; therefore, over the inevitable thou shouldst not grieve.
summary: Death is guaranteed for everything that takes birth, and new beginnings follow endings, making sorrow over life's natural cycles unnecessary.

siva_et: 2.28 Beings are unmanifested in their beginning, manifested in their middle state, O Arjuna, and unmanifested again in their end. What is there to grieve about?
summary: We come from the unseen, live in the visible world for a little while, and then return to the unseen—so why shed tears over this journey?

siva_et: 2.29 One sees This (the Self) as a wonder; another speaks of It as a wonder; another hears of It as a wonder; yet having heard, none understands It at all.
summary: The true nature of the soul is so deeply profound that witnessing or speaking of it feels like pure magic, yet it remains hard for the human mind to fully grasp.

siva_et: 2.30 This, the Indweller in the body of everyone, is ever indestructible, O Arjuna; therefore, thou shouldst not grieve for any creature.
summary: The life force dwelling within every living being can never truly be destroyed, meaning you don't need to carry heavy grief for anyone.

siva_et: 2.31 Further, having regard to thy duty, shouldst not waver, for there is nothing higher for a Kshatriya than a righteous war.
summary: Look straight at what is yours to do and don't let doubt shake you; standing up for what is right is the highest calling you can follow.

siva_et: 2.32 Happy are the Kshatriyas, O Arjuna! who are called upon to fight in such a battle that comes of itself as an open door to heaven.
summary: When a meaningful struggle lands right on your doorstep, see it as a rare and sacred opportunity to rise to your highest potential.

siva_et: 2.33 But if thou wilt not fight this righteous war, then having abandoned thine own duty and fame, thou shalt incur sin.
summary: If you walk away from your true responsibility out of hesitation, you turn your back on your integrity and lose your sense of honor.

siva_et: 2.34 People, too, will recount thy everlasting dishonour; and to one who has been honoured, dishonour is worse than death.
summary: Shunning your responsibility brings lasting shame, and for someone who values integrity, living with dishonor feels far worse than passing away.

siva_et: 2.35 The great car-warriors will think that thou hast withdrawn from the battle through fear; and thou wilt be lightly held by them who have thought much of thee.
summary: If you back down now, people who respect you will assume you ran away out of fear and will think far less of your character.

siva_et: 2.36 Thy enemies also, cavilling at thy power, will speak many abusive words. What is more painful than this?
summary: Hearing harsh criticisms and taunts from people who doubt your strength is a painful burden that hurts much deeper than physical pain.

siva_et: 2.37 Slain, thou wilt obtain heaven; victorious, thou wilt enjoy the earth; therefore, stand up, O son of Kunti, resolved to fight.
summary: Whatever the outcome—whether you stumble or succeed—stepping up to face your challenge brings deep fulfillment, so gather your courage and engage.

siva_et: 2.38 Having made pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat the same, engage thou in battle for the sake of battle; thus thou shalt not incur sin.
summary: When you treat success and failure, happiness and pain as the same, you can simply do what is right without anxiety over the outcome.

siva_et: 2.39 This, which has been taught to thee, is wisdon concerning Sankhya. Now listen to wisdom concerning Yoga, endowed with which, O Arjuna, thou shalt cast off the bonds of action.
summary: This timeless wisdom helps you understand life deeply and frees you from feeling trapped or bound by the heavy reactions of your actions.

siva_et: 2.40 In this there is no loss of effort, nor is there any harm (production of contrary results or transgression). Even a little of this knowledge (even a little practice of this Yoga) protects one from great fear.
summary: No effort on this spiritual path is ever wasted, and even a tiny step forward can shield you from deep anxiety and fear.

siva_et: 2.41 Here, O joy of the Kurus, there is but a single one-pointed determination; many-branched and endless are the thoughts of the irresolute.
summary: A focused, resolute mind stays steady on what truly matters, while an unsettled mind gets pulled in endless, confusing directions.

siva_et: 2.42 Flowery speech is uttered by the unwise, taking pleasure in the eulogising words of the Vedas, O Arjuna, saying, "There is nothing else."
summary: People caught up in worldly noise often chase superficial promises, missing the deeper truth of life.

siva_et: 2.43 Full of desires, having heaven as their goal, (they utter speech which is directed to ends) leading to new births as the result of their works, and prescribe various methods abounding in specific actions, for the attainment of pleasure and power.
summary: When your heart is entirely set on endless pleasures, rewards, and material gains, you trap yourself in a constant loop of wanting and rebirth.

siva_et: 2.44 For those who are attached to pleasure and power, whose minds are drawn away by such teaching, ï1thatï1 determinate reason is not formed which is steadily bent on meditation and Samadhi (superconscious state).
summary: If you are constantly distracted by the desire for pleasure and status, it becomes impossible to quiet your mind and find deep inner focus.

siva_et: 2.45 The Vedas deal with the three attributes (of Nature); be thou above these three attributes. O Arjuna, free yourself from the pairs of opposites, and ever remain in the ality of Sattva (goodness), freed from (the thought of) acisition and preservation, and be established in the Self.
summary: Rise above the endless pull of material life, let go of the constant need to acquire and protect things, and rest securely in your true self.

siva_et: 2.46 To the Brahmana who has known the Self, all the Vedas are of as much use as is a reservoir of water in a place where there is a flood.
summary: For someone who has awakened to their true inner self, ordinary religious rules and rituals become as unnecessary as a tiny puddle when a vast flood surrounds you.

siva_et: 2.47 Thy right is to work only, but never with its fruits; let not the fruits of action be thy motive, nor let thy attachment be to inaction.
summary: Focus purely on doing your work with care, but let go of needing a specific reward or outcome, and never choose to simply stop acting.

siva_et: 2.48 Perform action, O Arjuna, being steadfast in Yoga, abandoning attachment and balanced in success and failure. Evenness of mind is called Yoga.
summary: Stay grounded in your practice, do your part without clinging to results, and remain steady whether things go well or fall apart. True balance of mind is the heart of yoga.

siva_et: 2.49 Far lower than the Yoga of wisdon is action, O Arjuna. Seek thou refuge in wisdom; wretched are they whose motive is the fruit.
summary: Working just for the sake of a reward keeps you small; instead, anchor yourself in higher wisdom and act from a place of inner freedom.

siva_et: 2.50 Endowed with wisdom (evenness of mind), one casts off in this life both good and evil deeds; therefore, devote thyself to Yoga; Yoga is skill in action.
summary: When your mind is balanced in wisdom, you move beyond good and bad reactions, transforming everyday action into a true art of living.

siva_et: 2.51 The wise, possessed of knowledge, having abandoned the fruits of their actions, and being freed from the fetters of birth, go to the place which is beyond all evil.
summary: Wise souls who let go of the fruits of their actions break free from the cycles of struggle and rest in a place of complete peace beyond all suffering.

siva_et: 2.52 When thy intellect crosses beyond the mire of delusion, then thou shalt attain to indifference as to what has been heard and what has yet to be heard.
summary: When your mind finally clears the fog of confusion, you will stop getting caught up in endless information and opinions. True clarity lets you rest in peace beyond what you've heard or been taught.

siva_et: 2.53 When thy intellect, which is perplexed by the Veda text, which thou hast read, shall stand immovable and steady in the Self, then thou shalt attain Self-realisation.
summary: When your mind stops swaying back and forth from all the conflicting advice in the world and anchors deeply into your true self, you will find inner realization.

siva_et: 2.54 Arjuna said  What, O Krishna, is the description of him who has steady wisdom, and is merged in the superconscious state? How does one of steady wisdom speak, how does he sit, how does he walk?
summary: Arjuna asks how a truly wise and grounded person actually lives, speaks, and acts in daily life.

siva_et: 2.55 The Blessed Lord said  When a man completely casts off, O Arjuna, all the desires of the mind and is satisfied in the Self by the Self, then is he said to be one of steady wisdom.
summary: A truly wise person is one who lets go of anxious wanting and finds complete contentment resting within their own soul.

siva_et: 2.56 He whose mind is not shaken by adversity, who does not hanker after pleasures, and is free from attachment, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady wisdom.
summary: True wisdom means staying steady when life gets hard, not chasing cheap thrills, and remaining free from anxiety, fear, and sudden rage.

siva_et: 2.57 He who is everywhere without attachment, on meeting with anything good or bad, who neither rejoices not hastes, his wisdom is fixed.
summary: When you stop clinging tightly to outcomes, you remain calm and unshaken whether good things or bad things come your way.

siva_et: 2.58 When, like the tortoise which withdraws on all sides its limbs, he withdraws his senses from the sense-objects, then his wisdom becomes steady.
summary: Just like a turtle pulls its limbs inside for safety, true peace comes when you learn to gently draw your mind away from constant sensory distractions.

siva_et: 2.59 The objects of the senses turn away from the abstinent man leaving the longing (behind); but his longing also turns away on seeing the Supreme.
summary: You might force yourself to abstain from worldly temptations, but the craving often stays behind—until you experience a much deeper joy that completely heals that hunger.

siva_et: 2.60 The turbulent senses, O Arjuna, do violently carry away the mind of a wise man though he be striving (to control them).
summary: Even if you are trying your best, the pull of the senses can be so fierce that it forcibly drags your mind away.

siva_et: 2.61 Having restrained them all he should sit steadfast, intent on Me; his wisdom is steady whose senses are under control.
summary: By gently reining in your wild senses and anchoring your focus on the divine, your mind becomes steady and peaceful.

siva_et: 2.62 When a man thinks of the objects, attachment for them arises; from attachment desire is born; from desire anger arises.
summary: Dwelling on things leads to attachment, attachment breeds intense craving, and when those cravings are blocked, it turns straight into anger.

siva_et: 2.63 From anger comes delusion; from delusion loss of memory; from loss of memory the destruction of discrimination; from the destruction of discrimination he perishes.
summary: Anger clouds your judgment, making you forget who you are and losing your ability to make good choices—which ultimately leads to self-destruction.

siva_et: 2.64 But the self-controlled man, moving among the objects with the senses under restraint and free from attraction and repulsion, attains to peace.
summary: When you move through the world with your emotions in check, free from desperate cravings and strong aversions, you finally find deep peace.

siva_et: 2.65 In that peace all pains are destroyed; for the intellect of the tranil-minded soon becomes steady.
summary: In that quiet sanctuary of inner peace, all your pain and heartache melt away because your mind has finally found its anchor.

siva_et: 2.66 There is no knowledge of the Self to the unsteady and to the unsteady no meditation is possible, and to the unmeditative there can be no peace, and to the man who has no peace, how can there be happiness?
summary: When your mind is constantly scattered and unsettled, finding inner calm and true happiness becomes nearly impossible.

siva_et: 2.67 For the mind, which follows in the wake of the wandering senses, carries away his discrimination, as the wind (carries away) a boat on the waters.
summary: Allowing your mind to blindly chase every passing impulse and desire will quickly sweep away your better judgment, like a boat caught in a storm.

siva_et: 2.68 Therefore, O mighty-armed Arjuna, his knowledge is steady whose senses are completely restrained from sense-objects.
summary: True wisdom and steadiness come when you learn to gently pull your attention away from the constant pull of external distractions.

siva_et: 2.69 That which is night to all beings, in that the self-controlled man is awake; when all beings are awake, that is night for the Muni (sage) who sees.
summary: The spiritually awake person lives differently from the crowd, finding clarity where others are blind and peace where others rush.

siva_et: 2.70 He attains peace into whom all desires enter as waters enter the ocean which, filled from all sides, remains unmoved; but not the man who is full of desires.
summary: True peace belongs to the person who remains unshakable inside, even as desires wash over them like rivers flowing into a vast, steady ocean.

siva_et: 2.71 That man attains peace who, abandoning all desires, moves about without longing, without the sense of mine and without egoism.
summary: Real peace comes when you let go of constant craving, possessiveness, and the heavy burden of ego.

siva_et: 2.72 This is the Brahmic seat (eternal state), O son of Pritha. Attaining to this, none is deluded. Being established therein, even at the end of life, one attains to oneness with Brahman.
summary: Reaching this divine state frees you from all confusion and delusion, allowing you to rest in timeless peace even at the very end of life.

siva_et: 3.1 Arjuna said  If Thou thinkest that knowledge is superior to action, O Krishna, why then, O Kesava, dost Thou ask me to engage in this terrible action?
summary: Arjuna is confused and asks why Krishna is pushing him into a difficult, painful conflict if spiritual wisdom is truly what matters most.

siva_et: 3.2 With this apparently perplexing speech, Thou confusest, as it were, my understanding; therefore tell me that one way for certain by which I may attain bliss.
summary: Feeling completely overwhelmed and mixed up by these deep teachings, Arjuna begs for one clear and simple path forward.

siva_et: 3.3 The Blessed Lord said  In this world there is a twofold path, as I said before, O sinless one; the path of knowledge of the Sankhyas and the path of action of the Yogins.
summary: Krishna explains that there are two complementary paths in life: the path of deep inner wisdom and the path of active, engaged living.

siva_et: 3.4 Not by non-performance of actions does man reach actionlessness; nor by mere renunciation does he attain to perfection.
summary: You cannot escape your responsibilities or reach true maturity simply by avoiding action or trying to run away from life.

siva_et: 3.5 Verily none can ever remain for even a moment without performing action; for everyone is made to act helplessly indeed by the alities born of Nature.
summary: No one can ever truly stop acting completely, because we are all constantly shaped and driven by the natural energies of life.

siva_et: 3.6 He who, restraining the organs of action, sits thinking of the sense-objects in mind, he of deluded understanding is called a hypocrite.
summary: Pretending to be detached on the outside while your mind secretly obsesses over things you want is just self-deception.

siva_et: 3.7 But whosoever, controlling the senses by the mind, O Arjuna, engages himself in Karma Yoga with the organs of action, without attachment, he excels.
summary: True greatness belongs to the person who manages their mind, takes up their responsibilities, and acts selflessly without clinging to the results.

siva_et: 3.8 Do thou perform (thy) bounden duty, for action is superior to inaction and even the maintenance of the body would not be possible for thee by inaction.
summary: Keep moving forward and doing what you have to do, because staying stuck or inactive won't even help you take care of your basic needs.

siva_et: 3.9 The world is bound by actions other than those performed for the sake of sacrifice; do thou, therefore, O son of Kunti (Arjuna), perform action for that sake (for sacrifice alone), free from attachment.
summary: Take care of your responsibilities, but try to let go of needing a specific outcome or reward from your efforts.

siva_et: 3.10 The Creator, having in the beginning (of creation) created mankind together with sacrifice, said, "By this shall ye propagate; let this be the milch cow of your desires (the cow which yields all the desired objects)."
summary: Life is designed for us to support one another and nurture our shared well-being rather than just chasing selfish wants.

siva_et: 3.11 With this do ye nourish the gods and may those gods nourish you; thus nourishing one another, ye shall attain to the highest good.
summary: When we give back to the world and support the forces of life, life will take care of us in return, leading us to peace.

siva_et: 3.12 The gods, nourished by the sacrifice, will give you the desired objects. So, he who enjoys the objects given by the gods without offering (in return) to them, is verily a thief.
summary: It's unfair to just take from the universe without ever giving back or showing appreciation for the blessings you receive.

siva_et: 3.13 The righteous who eat the remnants of the sacrifice are freed from all sins; but those sinful ones who cook food (only) for their own sake verily eat sin.
summary: When we share what we have and live with a spirit of service, we free our minds from guilt and heaviness.

siva_et: 3.14 From food come forth beings; from rain food is produced; from sacrifice arises rain and sacrifice is born of action.
summary: Everything in nature is connected in a continuous cycle of life, nourishment, and action.

siva_et: 3.15 Know thou that action comes from Brahma and Brahma comes from the Imperishable. Therefore, the all-pervading (Brahma) ever rests in sacrifice.
summary: At the very heart of creation is a divine order rooted in selfless action and giving.

siva_et: 3.16 He who does not follow here the wheel thus set revolving, who is of sinful life, rejoicing in the senses, he lives in vain, O Arjuna.
summary: Getting lost only in sensory pleasures while ignoring your wider responsibilities makes life feel empty and wasted.

siva_et: 3.17 But for that man who rejoices only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self and who is content in the Self alone, verily there is nothing to do.
summary: When you find deep contentment and peace within your true self, the frantic need to constantly chase things fades away.

siva_et: 3.18 For him there is no interest whatever in what is done or what is not done; nor does he depend on any being for any object.
summary: A truly centered person isn't shaken by successes or failures, and they don't rely on others to feel complete.

siva_et: 3.19 Therefore without attachment, do thou always perform action which should be done; for by performing action without attachment man reaches the Supreme.
summary: Focus on doing what is right simply because it's right, letting go of the stress of outcomes, and you will find profound fulfillment.

siva_et: 3.20 Janaka and others attained perfection verily by action only; even with a view to the protection of the masses thou shouldst perform action.
summary: Wise leaders of the past found their highest fulfillment through action, and you should keep working for the good of others too.

siva_et: 3.21 Whatsoever a great man does, that the other men also do; whatever he sets up as the standard, that the world (mankind) follows.
summary: People look up to those around them and follow their example, so try to lead with integrity in whatever you do.

siva_et: 3.22 There is nothing in the three worlds, O Arjuna, that should be done by Me, nor is there anything unattained that should be attained; yet I engage Myself in action.
summary: Even though the Divine has nothing left to gain or achieve, He still acts continuously for the sake of the world, setting the ultimate example for us.

siva_et: 3.23 For, should I not ever engage Myself in action, unwearied, men would in every way follow My path, O Arjuna.
summary: If you stopped showing up and doing your part, others would lose their way; your actions matter as an example to those around you.

siva_et: 3.24 These worlds would perish if I did not perform action; I should be the author of confusion of castes and destruction of these beings.
summary: If we all abandoned our responsibilities and stopped trying, the world would fall apart into chaos and confusion. Your contribution is vital.

siva_et: 3.25 As the ignorant men act from attachment to action, O Bharata (Arjuna), so should the wise act without attachment, wishing the welfare of the world.
summary: While everyday people work hard just to get what they want, wise people work with the exact same dedication—only driven by love and a desire to help others, not personal gain.

siva_et: 3.26 Let no wise man unsettle the mind of ignorant people who are attached to action; he should engage them in all actions, himself fulfilling them with devotion.
summary: Don't shake the confidence of those still learning; instead, lead by example and show them how to throw themselves fully and joyfully into whatever needs to be done.

siva_et: 3.27 All actions are wrought in all cases by the alities of Nature only. He whose mind is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer."
summary: Everything in this world happens naturally through the forces of nature, but our ego tricks us into proudly believing, 'I am the one doing all this.'

siva_et: 3.28 But he who knows the Truth, O mighty-armed (Arjuna), about the divisions of the alities and (their) functions, knowing that the Gunas as senses move amidst the Gunas as the sense-objects, is not attached.
summary: When you truly understand how your mind and senses interact with the world, you stop getting caught up in the drama and remain peacefully unattached.

siva_et: 3.29 Those deluded by the alities of Nature are attached to the functions of the alities. The man of perfect knowledge should not unsettle the foolish one who is of imperfect knowledge.
summary: People who are caught up in sensory distractions need patience, not judgment; a grounded person gently guides them without disturbing their peace.

siva_et: 3.30 Renouncing all actions in Me, with the mind centred in the Self, free from hope and egoism, and from (mental) fever, do thou fight.
summary: Lay all your burdens and expectations at the feet of the Divine, quiet your anxious mind, let go of your ego, and simply dive into the battle of life.

siva_et: 3.31 Those men who constantly practise this teaching of Mine with faith and without cavilling, they too are freed from actions.
summary: If you trust these words and practice them with an open heart rather than cynicism, you will finally break free from the heavy burden of past karma.

siva_et: 3.32 But those who carp at My teaching and do not practise it, deluded of all knowledge, and devoid of discrimination, know them to be doomed to destruction.
summary: When you constantly pick apart good advice out of cynicism and refuse to try it, you stay stuck in confusion and miss out on true growth.

siva_et:
3.33 Even a wise man acts in accordance with his own nature; beings will follow Nature; what can 
restraint do?
summary: Even smart people tend to default to their ingrained habits and nature, so fighting yourself with harsh suppression rarely works—true growth takes patient guidance.

siva_et: 3.34 Attachment and aversion for the objects of the senses abide in the senses; let none come under their sway; for, they are his foes.
summary: Cravings and frustrations will always whisper to your senses, but don't let them take the steering wheel—they are your truest and most dangerous inner enemies.

siva_et: 3.35 Better is one's own duty, though devoid of merit than the duty of another well discharged. Better is death in one's own duty; the duty of another is fraught with fear (is productive of danger).
summary: It is always better to stumble through your own authentic path and responsibilities than to try living someone else's life, which is full of anxiety and fear.

siva_et: 3.36 Arjuna said  But impelled by what does man commit sin, though against his wishes, O Varshneya (Krishna), constrained as it were, by force?
summary: Arjuna asks why people end up doing things they never intended to do, driven by some invisible force. It's that familiar feeling of wondering why we sabotaged ourselves against our own better judgment.

siva_et: 3.37 The Blessed Lord said  It is desire, it is anger both of the ality of Rajas, all-devouring, all-sinful; know this as the foe here (in this world).
summary: Krishna reveals that the true inner enemy is our own unbridled desire and anger, which consume everything in their path. Recognizing what's really driving your frustration is the first step to freeing yourself from it.

siva_et: 3.38 As fire is enveloped by smoke, as a mirror by dust, and as an embryo by the amnion, so is this enveloped by that.
summary: Just as smoke hides a fire or dust covers a mirror, our inner clarity can get completely clouded over by cravings. When you feel foggy and confused, know that it's just a temporary film covering your true wisdom.

siva_et: 3.39 O Arjuna, wisdom is enveloped by this constant enemy of the wise in the form of desire, which is unappeasable as fire.
summary: Our clear judgment is constantly blocked by a relentless hunger for things that can never truly satisfy us. This insatiable craving is the silent thief robbing you of your peace of mind.

siva_et: 3.40 The senses, the mind and the intellect are said to be its seat; through these it deludes the embodied by veiling his wisdom.
summary: This relentless craving takes up residence in your senses, mind, and intellect, tricking you into losing touch with your true self. It explains why our own thoughts and impulses can suddenly feel like they are working against us.

siva_et: 3.41 Therefore, O best of the Bharatas (Arjuna), controlling the senses first, do thou kill this sinful thing, the destroyer of knowledge and realisation.
summary: Take charge by learning to quiet your wandering senses and impulses before they pull you off track. Taming these urges is essential to protecting your inner peace and clarity.

siva_et: 3.42 They say that the senses are superior (to the body); superior to the senses is the mind; superior to the mind is the intellect; one who is superior even to the intellect is He (the Self).
summary: There is a hierarchy to your inner world: your physical body and senses are deep, but your mind is subtler, your intellect is deeper still, and your true spiritual self lies beyond them all. Remembering who you really are helps you step back from turbulent thoughts.

siva_et: 3.43 Thus knowing Him Who is superior to the intellect and restraining the self by the Self, slay thou, O mighty-armed Arjuna, the enemy in the form of desire, hard to coner.
summary: Anchor yourself in your deeper spiritual identity to master your own mind and overcome the hard-to-fight urges of desire. You have the inner strength to conquer whatever emotional turbulence is holding you back.

siva_et: 4.1 The Blessed Lord said  I taught this imperishable Yoga to Vivasvan; he told it to Manu; Manu proclaimed it to Ikshvaku.
summary: Krishna explains that this timeless path of spiritual wisdom has been passed down through the ages. You are tapping into an ancient, unbroken tradition of truth when you seek deeper meaning.

siva_et: 4.2 This, handed down thus in regular succession, the royal sages knew. This Yoga, by long lapse of time, has been lost here, O Parantapa (burner of the foes).
summary: Over time, profound spiritual truths can fade and get lost in the noise of the world. Rediscovering them requires a deliberate return to what truly matters.

siva_et: 4.3 That same ancient Yoga has been today taught to thee by Me, for thou art My devotee and My friend; it is the supreme secret.
summary: Krishna shares this profound wisdom because of the close bond of friendship and trust they share. When you open your heart, deep guidance naturally finds its way to you.

siva_et: 4.4 Arjuna said  Later on was Thy birth, and prior to it was the birth of Vivasvan (the Sun); how am I to understand that Thou taughtest this Yoga in the beginning?
summary: Arjuna is understandably confused by the timeline, wondering how Krishna could have taught someone who lived ages ago. It is completely normal to question things that don't immediately make logical sense.

siva_et: 4.5 The Blessed Lord said  Many births of Mine have passed as well as of thine, O Arjuna; I know them all but thou knowest not, O Parantapa (scorcher of foes).
summary: Krishna gently reminds Arjuna that while we cycle through many lifetimes and forget our pasts, the divine sees the whole picture. There is a much larger tapestry at play than what we can perceive right now.

siva_et: 4.6 Though I am unborn, of imperishable nature, and though I am the Lord of all beings, yet, governing My own Nature, I am born by My own Maya.
summary: Though truly timeless and unbound by human limitations, the divine manifests in the world through its own magical power. This reminds us that there is an eternal reality quietly operating beneath the surface of our changing lives.

siva_et: 4.7 Whenever there is decline of righteousness, O Arjuna, and rise of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself.
summary: Whenever goodness struggles and unfairness takes over, the Divine steps right into the world to restore balance.

siva_et: 4.8 For the protection of the good, for the destruction of the wicked and for the establishment of righteousness, I am born in every age.
summary: You are never truly forgotten or unprotected; whenever life feels overwhelmed by hardship, the divine presence steps in to guide justice and shelter the good.

siva_et: 4.9 He who thus know, in their true light, My divine birth and action, having abandoned the body, is not born again, he comes to Me, O Arjuna.
summary: When you truly understand the divine nature of life and action, you break free from endless struggle and find your way home to lasting peace.

siva_et: 4.10 Freed from attachment, fear and anger, absorbed in Me, taking refuge in Me, purified by the fire of knowledge, many have attained to My Being.
summary: By letting go of your anxieties, letting go of anger, and anchoring your heart in the divine, you can heal and find deep, lasting peace.

siva_et: 4.11 In whatever way men approach Me even so do I reward them; My path do men tread in all ways, O Arjuna.
summary: However you reach out for help—no matter your path or your struggle—the Divine meets you right where you are.

siva_et: 4.12 Those who long for success in action in this world sacrifice to the gods; because success is ickly attained by men through action.
summary: People often chase quick rewards and success in the material world because results can come so fast when we put in the effort.

siva_et: 4.13 The fourfold caste has been created by Me according to the differentiation of Guna and Karma; though I am the author thereof know Me as non-doer and immutable.
summary: Even though human traits and roles are woven into the fabric of life, the deepest part of you remains untouched and free from worldly labels.

siva_et: 4.14 Actions do not taint Me, nor have I a desire for the fruit of actions. He who knows Me thus is not bound by actions.
summary: When you act without constantly craving rewards, the stress of your actions won't stick to you, leaving your mind clear and free.

siva_et: 4.15 Having known this, the ancient seekers after freedom also performed action; therefore do thou also perform action, as did the ancients in days of yore.
summary: Knowing that freedom is possible, those who came before us still did their daily work—and so should you, stepping up to your responsibilities.

siva_et: 4.16 What is action? What is inaction? As to this even the wise are confused. Therefore I shall teach thee such action (the nature of action and inaction) by knowing which thou shalt be liberated from the evil (of Samsara, the wheel of birth and death).
summary: Even wise people sometimes get tangled up trying to figure out what is right to do, which is why a clearer understanding helps free you from confusion and pain.

siva_et:
4.17 For verily (the true nature) of action (enjoined by the scriptures) should be known, also (that) 
of forbidden (or unlawful) action, and of inaction; hard to understand is the nature (path) of action.
summary: Understanding how to act rightly—and knowing what choices to avoid—can be complicated, but figuring it out is a crucial part of your journey.

siva_et: 4.18 He who seeth inaction in action and action in inaction, he is wise among men; he is a Yogi and performer of all actions.
summary: True wisdom is finding stillness in the middle of busy action, and remaining active while keeping a calm, unattached heart.

siva_et: 4.19 He whose undertakings are all devoid of desires and (selfish) purposes and whose actions have been burnt by the fire of knowledge,  him the wise call a sage.
summary: A truly wise person acts purely, letting go of selfish cravings and personal demands, burning away old mental habits with clear understanding.

siva_et: 4.20 Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of the action, ever content, depending on nothing, he does not do anything though engaged in activity.
summary: When you stop clinging to the results of your work and find contentment within yourself, you stay peaceful and centered no matter how busy life gets.

siva_et: 4.21 Without hope and with the mind and the self controlled, having abandoned all covetousness, doing mere bodily action, he incurs no sin.
summary: When you let go of selfish cravings and keep your desires in check, you free yourself from the heavy burden of negative karma.

siva_et: 4.22 Content with what comes to him without effort, free from the pairs of opposites and envy, even-minded in success and failure, though acting, he is not bound.
summary: True freedom comes from accepting whatever life brings your way and staying balanced through both wins and losses without getting shaken.

siva_et: 4.23 To one who is devoid of attchment, who is liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge, who works for the sake of sacrifice (for the sake of God), the whole action is dissolved.
summary: When you act purely out of love and duty rather than attachment to the results, all your mental baggage simply melts away.

siva_et: 4.24 Brahman is the oblation; Brahman is the melted butter (ghee); by Brahman is the oblation poured into the fire of Brahman; Brahman verily shall be reached by him who always sees Brahman in action.
summary: When you shift your perspective, you begin to see the divine presence alive in every single action and moment of your daily life.

siva_et: 4.25 Some Yogies perform sacrifice to the gods alone; while others (who have realised the Self) offer the self as sacrifice by the Self in the fire of Brahman alone.
summary: Some people find peace through devotion, while others find it by completely offering their individual ego into the fire of the divine Self.

siva_et: 4.26 Some again offer the organ of hearing and other senses as sacrifice in the fire of restraint; others offer sound and other objects of the senses as sacrifice in the fire of the senses.
summary: Practicing self-restraint helps you master your senses, keeping you grounded instead of being constantly pulled around by external distractions.

siva_et: 4.27 Others again sacrifice all the functions of the senses and those of the breath (vital energy or Prana) in the fire of the Yoga of self-restraint kindled by knowledge.
summary: By pairing self-awareness with deep discipline, you learn to quiet the restless fluctuations of your mind and life force.

siva_et: 4.28 Others again offer wealth, austerity and Yoga as sacrifice, while the ascetics of self-restraint and rigid vows offer study of scriptures and knowledge as sacrifice.
summary: People dedicate themselves to growth in different ways—whether through generous giving, spiritual discipline, or the pursuit of sacred knowledge.

siva_et: 4.29 Others offer as sacrifice the outgoing breath in the incoming, and the incoming in the outgoing, restraining the course of the outgoing and the incoming breaths, solely absorbed in the restraint of the breath.
summary: By learning to steady your breath and inward focus, you can quiet the storm of thoughts running through your head.

siva_et: 4.30 Others who regulate their diet offer life-breaths in life-breaths. All these are knowers of sacrifice, whose sins are destroyed by sacrifice.
summary: Every intentional act of discipline and mindful living helps clear away the inner clutter weighing down your spirit.

siva_et: 4.31 Those who eat the remnants of the sacrifice, which are like nectar, go to the eternal Brahman. This world is not for the man who does not perform sacrifice; how then can he have the other, O Arjuna?
summary: Living a life of selfless sharing and devotion nourishes your soul and opens the door to lasting peace.

siva_et: 4.32 Thus, manifold sacrifices are spread out before Brahman (literally) at the mouth or face of Brahman). Know them all as born of action and thus knowing, thou shalt be liberated.
summary: There are many different paths of mindful action available to you, and understanding them brings a deep sense of inner liberation.

siva_et: Swami Sivananda did not comment on this sloka
summary: This verse is a placeholder where commentary was not provided, but it reminds us to seek clarity when we feel stuck.

siva_et: 4.34 Know That by long prostration, by estion and by service; the wise who have realised the Truth will instruct thee in (that) knowledge.
summary: When you feel lost, don't hesitate to humbly approach wise guides and mentors who can help light the way forward.

siva_et: 4.35 Knowing ï1thatï1 thou shalt not, O Arjuna, again get deluded like this; and by that thou shalt see all beings in thy Self and also in Me.
summary: When you truly understand your connection to the divine, you'll see yourself in everyone and never feel lost or confused again.

siva_et: 4.36 Even if thou art the most sinful of all sinners, yet thou shalt verily cross all sins by the raft of knowledge.
summary: No matter how many mistakes you've made or how heavy your past feels, true self-understanding can carry you past it all.

siva_et: 4.37 As the blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes.
summary: Just like a blazing fire burns wood to ash, the light of true wisdom burns away the heavy burden of your past actions and karma.

siva_et: 4.38 Verily, there is no purifier in this world like knowledge. He who is perfected in Yoga finds it in the Self in time.
summary: There is nothing more cleansing in this life than true wisdom; keep practicing and you will discover it naturally within yourself.

siva_et: 4.39 The man who is full of faith, who is devoted to it, and who has subdued the senses obtains (this) knowledge; and having obtained the knowledge he attains at once to the supreme peace.
summary: If you trust the process, stay devoted, and quiet your restless senses, peace will find you when you gain true understanding.

siva_et: 4.40 The ignorant the faithless, the doubting self goes to destruction; there is neither this world nor the other, nor happiness for the doubting.
summary: Constant doubt and a lack of faith can trap you in a cycle of misery, making it impossible to find true happiness anywhere.

siva_et: 4.41 He who has renounced actions by Yoga, whose doubts are rent asunder by knowledge, and who is self-possessed  actions do not bind him, O Arjuna.
summary: When your doubts are cleared by wisdom and you act with inner balance, the consequences of your actions won't weigh you down.

siva_et: 4.42 Therefore with the sword of the knowledge (of the Self) cut asunder the doubt of the self born of ignorance, residing in thy heart, and take refuge in Yoga. Arise, O Arjuna.
summary: Cut through your inner confusion with the sharp sword of self-awareness, ground yourself in practice, and step forward with courage.

siva_et: 5.1 Arjuna said  Renunciation of actions, O Krishna, Thou praisest, and again Yoga. Tell me conclusively that which is the better of the two.
summary: Arjuna is feeling torn between two different paths of spiritual life, asking Krishna to simply tell him which one is right.

siva_et: 5.2 The Blessed Lord said  Renunciation and the Yoga of action both lead to the highest bliss; but of the two, the Yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action.
summary: While both withdrawing from the world and actively engaging in it lead to peace, diving in and doing your daily duty is the more practical path.

siva_et: 5.3 He should be known as a perpertual Sannyasi who neither hates nor desires; for, free from the pairs of opposites, O mighty-armed Arjuna, he is easily set free from bondage.
summary: True freedom isn't about running away from life; it's about living without being chained to your cravings or aversions.

siva_et: 5.4 Children, not the wise, speak of knowledge and the Yoga of action or the performance of action as though they are distinct and different; he who is truly established in one obtains the fruits of both.
summary: Immature people argue about which spiritual path is best, but wise people know that fully committing to any true practice brings you to the same destination.

siva_et: 5.5 That place which is reached by the Sankhyas or the Jnanis is reached by the Yogis (Karma Yogis). He sees, who sees knowledge and the performance of action (Karma Yoga) as one.
summary: The ultimate state of peace is the same whether you find it through quiet contemplation or by actively doing your work in the world.

siva_et: 5.6 But renunciation, O mighty-armed Arjuna, is hard to attain without Yoga; the Yoga-harmonised sage ickly goes to Brahman.
summary: Trying to completely abandon the world and detach by force is exhausting, but when you practice mindful action, peace comes to you quickly.

siva_et: 5.7 He who is devoted to the path of action, whose mind is ite pure, who has conered the self, who has subdued his senses and who realises his Self as the Self in all beings, though acting, is not tainted.
summary: When you purify your mind and master your senses, you can live and act in the world without being weighed down by negativity.

siva_et: 5.8 "I do nothing at all," thus would the harmonised knower of Truth think  seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, going, sleeping, breathing.
summary: Even while going about your everyday physical routines, a centered mind quietly knows that your true self is just observing, not trapped by the hustle.

siva_et: 5.9 Speaking, letting go, seizing, opening and closing the eyes  convinced that the senses move among the sense-objects.
summary: Recognize that your senses naturally interact with the world around you, and you don't have to get tangled up in every mental reaction.

siva_et: 5.10 He who does actions, offering them to Brahman, and abandoning attachment, is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus-leaf is not tainted by water.
summary: Offer your daily efforts up to a higher purpose and let go of obsessive outcomes, allowing you to glide through stress like water off a lotus leaf.

siva_et: 5.11 Yogis, having abandoned attachment, perform actions only by the body, mind, intellect, and even by the senses, for the purification of the self.
summary: When you drop your anxious attachments, your work becomes a gentle practice for purifying your heart and finding inner clarity.

siva_et: 5.12 The united one (the well poised or the harmonised) having abandoned the fruit of action attains to the eternal peace: the non-united only (the unsteady or the unbalanced) impelled by desire, attached to the fruit, is bound.
summary: True, lasting peace comes when you stop obsessing over the results of your efforts, whereas constantly chasing rewards only keeps you stressed and bound.

siva_et: 5.13 Mentally renouncing all actions and self-controlled, the embodied one rests happily in the nine-gated city, neither acting nor causing others (body and senses) to act.
summary: By gently stepping back from mental turmoil and taking control of your inner space, you can rest quietly inside yourself, free from unnecessary strain.

siva_et: 5.14 Neither agency nor actions does the Lord create for the world, nor union with the fruits of actions. But it is Nature that acts.
summary: Life unfolds naturally through its own patterns; you don't carry the crushing weight of engineering every single outcome in the universe.

siva_et: 5.15 The Lord takes neither the demerit nor even the merit of any; knowledge is enveloped by ignorance, thery beings are deluded.
summary: Life doesn't judge or keep score against you; we often feel lost and heavy simply because we've temporarily forgotten our true, luminous nature.

siva_et: 5.16 But to those whose ignorance is destroyed by the knowledge of the Self, like the sun, knowledge reveals the Supreme (Brahman).
summary: When self-understanding dawns within you, it clears away the fog of confusion like the morning sun chasing away the dark.

siva_et: 5.17 Their intellect absorbed in That, their self being That, established in That, with That for their supreme goal, they go whence there is no return, their sins dispelled by knowledge.
summary: Fixing your heart and ultimate goals on the Divine clears away your inner turbulence and leads you home to a place of permanent peace.

siva_et: 5.18 Sages look with an eal eye on a Brahmana endowed with learning and humility, on a cow, on an elephant, and even on a dog and an outcaste.
summary: Wise souls look past superficial labels and see the same sacred spark of life in every single living being.

siva_et: 5.19 Even here (in this world) birth (everything) is overcome by those whose minds rest in eality; Brahman is spotless indeed and eal; therefore they are established in Brahman.
summary: Even right here in the middle of a chaotic world, keeping your mind anchored in steady truth allows you to rise above life's constant ups and downs.

siva_et: 5.20 Resting in Brahman, with steady intellect and undeluded, the knower of Brahman neither rejoiceth on obtaining what is pleasant nor grieveth on obtaining what is unpleasant.
summary: When your mind is truly steady, you stop getting thrown off balance by getting what you dislike or losing what you love, finding a deep, unshakable calm.

siva_et: 5.21 With the self unattached to external contacts he finds happiness in the Self; with the self engaged in    the meditation of Brahman he attains to the endless happiness.
summary: When you stop searching for happiness in the outside world and look within, you'll find a deep, lasting peace that never fades.

siva_et: 5.22 The enjoyments that are born of contacts are only generators of pain, for they have a beginning and an end, O Arjuna; the wise man does not rejoice in them.
summary: Chasing temporary pleasures usually leads to heartache in the end, because nothing in the material world lasts forever. True wisdom is learning not to depend on them for your happiness.

siva_et: 5.23 He who is able, while still here (in this world) to withstand, before the liberation from the body, the impulse born out of desire and anger  he is a Yogi, he is a happy man.
summary: True inner strength means learning to manage the sudden urges of desire and frustration before they overwhelm you. Master that, and you'll find a steady, unshakeable peace.

siva_et: 5.24 He who is happy within, who rejoices within, and who is illuminated within, that Yogi attains absolute freedom or Moksha, himself becoming Brahman.
summary: When your joy and light come from a deep place inside you rather than external things, you become truly free and at one with the universe.

siva_et: 5.25 The sages (Rishis) obtain absolute freedom or Moksha  they whose sins have been destroyed, whose dualities (perception of dualities or experience of the pairs of opposites) are torn asunder, who are self-controlled, and intent on the welfare of all beings.
summary: Absolute freedom comes to those who master their minds, move past life's constant ups and downs, and genuinely care about the well-being of everyone around them.

siva_et: 5.26 Absolute freedom (or Brahmic bliss) exists on all sides for those self-controlled ascetics who are free from desire and anger, who have controlled their thoughts and who have realised the Self.
summary: If you can quiet your anger, let go of greedy cravings, and truly understand who you are inside, peace and freedom are all around you, waiting for you to claim them.

siva_et: 5.27 Shutting out (all) external contacts and fixing the gaze between the eyrow, ealising the outgoing and incoming breaths moving within the nostrils.
summary: By gently turning your attention away from distractions and focusing on your breath, you can quiet a restless mind and find your center.

siva_et: 5.28 With the senses, the mind and the intellect (ever) controlled, having liberation as his supreme goal, free from desire, fear and anger  the sage is verily liberated for ever.
summary: When you finally take charge of your senses and mind, letting go of fear, anger, and chasing desires, you step into a state of permanent peace.

siva_et: 5.29 He who knows Me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great Lord of all the worlds and the friend of all beings, attains to peace.
summary: Realize that you are supported by a loving presence who is the true friend of all living beings, and your heart will finally rest in peace.

siva_et: 6.1 The Blessed Lord said  He who performs his bounden duty without depending on the fruits of his actions  he is a Sannyasi and a Yogi; not he who is without fire and without action.
summary: True spiritual practice isn't about running away from your responsibilities; it's about showing up and doing what's right without obsessing over the results.

siva_et: 6.2 Do thou, O Arjuna, know Yoga to be that which they call renunciation; no one verily becomes a Yogi who has not renounced thoughts.
summary: True yoga is about letting go of selfish motives and silencing the endless chatter in your mind. You can't find inner peace while your thoughts are constantly running the show.

siva_et: 6.3 For a sage who wishes to attain to Yoga, action is said to be the means; for the same sage who has attained to Yoga, inaction (iescence) is said to be the means.
summary: Action is the necessary stepping stone when you are trying to grow and find your center, but once you've truly arrived at inner peace, stillness becomes your natural state.

siva_et: 6.4 When a man is not attached to the sense-objects or to actions, having renounced all thoughts, then he is said to have attained to Yoga.
summary: When you no longer depend on worldly things or personal rewards to feel fulfilled, and you quiet your restless thoughts, you have truly mastered the art of yoga.

siva_et: 6.5 One should raise oneself by one's Self alone; let not one lower oneself; for the Self alone is the friend of oneself, and the Self alone is the enemy of oneself.
summary: You are your own greatest ally or your own worst obstacle—pull yourself up with your own mind rather than letting your thoughts drag you down.

siva_et: 6.6 The Self is the friend of the self of him by whom the self has been conered by the Self, but to the unconered self, this Self stands in the position of an enemy, like an (external) foe.
summary: Your own mind can be your greatest friend or your toughest opponent, depending on whether you've learned to master it. When you take charge of your inner world, you find a reliable ally within.

siva_et: 6.7 The Supreme Self of him who is self-controlled and peaceful is balanced in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, as also in honour and dishonour.
summary: When you find true peace within, life's ups and downs—praise and criticism, joy and pain—stop knocking you off balance. You remain steady and centered no matter what comes your way.

siva_et: 6.8 The Yogi who is satisfied with the knowledge and the wisdom (of the Self), who has conered the senses, and to whom a clod of earth, a piece of stone and gold are the same, is said to be harmonied (i.e., is said to have attained Nirvikalpa Samadhi).
summary: True wealth isn't about material possessions like gold versus dirt; it's the inner richness of wisdom and self-mastery. When you are fulfilled inside, external treasures lose their grip on you.

siva_et: 6.9 He who is of the same mind to the good-hearted, friends, enemies, the indifferent, the neutral, the hateful, the relatives, the righteous and the unrighteous, excels.
summary: True spiritual maturity means treating everyone with the same open heart—whether they are friends, rivals, or strangers. Rise above personal biases and drama to see the bigger picture of human connection.

siva_et: 6.10 Let the Yogi try constantly to keep the mind steady, remaining in solitude, alone, with the mind and the body controlled, and free from hope and covetousness.
summary: Quiet your mind by stepping back from constant longing and mental clutter. Finding a calm, solitary space helps you anchor your thoughts and cultivate lasting steadiness.

siva_et: 6.11 In a clean spot, having established a firm seat of his own, neither too high nor too low, made of a cloth, a skin and Kusa-grass, one over the other.
summary: Creating a dedicated, comfortable physical space helps set the right tone for inner work and meditation. Simple preparation honors the sacred time you take for yourself.

siva_et: 6.12 There, having made the mind one-pointed, with the actions of the mind and the senses controlled, let him, seated on the seat, practise Yoga for the purification of the self.
summary: Gently gather your scattered senses and focus your mind on a single point. This intentional practice purifies your thoughts and brings deep inner calm.

siva_et: 6.13 Let him firmly hold his body, head and neck erect and still, gazing at the tip of his nose, without looking around.
summary: Sitting upright and steady in your body helps signal stability to your mind. Simple physical posture is a wonderful tool to ground your awareness and stop distractions.

siva_et: 6.14 Serene-minded, fearless, firm in the vow of a Brahmachari, having controlled the mind, thinking of Me and balanced in mind, let him sit, having Me as his supreme goal.
summary: Let go of fear and anchor your mind in a place of higher purpose. When your heart is steady and focused on the divine, a deep, fearless peace takes over.

siva_et: 6.15 Thus always keeping the mind balanced, the Yogi, with the mind controlled, attains to the peace abiding in Me, which culminates in liberation.
summary: By gently reining in a restless mind day after day, you unlock a profound, lasting peace. This steady inner calm leads you straight to ultimate freedom and joy.

siva_et: 6.16 Verily Yoga is not possible for him who eats too much, nor for him who does not eat at all, nor for him who sleeps too much, nor for him who is (always) awake, O Arjuna.
summary: True balance isn't found in extremes of overindulgence or harsh deprivation. Taking care of your basic rhythms—eating and resting mindfully—is essential for mental clarity.

siva_et:
6.17 Yoga becomes the destroyer of pain for him who is moderate in eating and recreation (such 
as walking, etc.), who is moderate in exertion in actions, who is moderate in sleep and wakefulness.
summary: When you keep your habits, sleep, and efforts moderate and balanced, much of life's unnecessary struggle simply melts away. Self-care and mindful pacing are the true antidotes to exhaustion.

siva_et: 6.18 When the perfectly controlled mind rests in the Self only, free from longing for all the objects of desires, then it is said, 'He is united'.
summary: When your mind finally rests in your true self instead of chasing endless external wants, you achieve a deep and harmonious union. Letting go of constant craving brings profound stillness.

siva_et: 6.19 As a lamp placed in a windless spot does not flicker  to such is compared the Yogi of controlled mind, practising Yoga in the Self (or absorbed in the Yoga of the Self).
summary: Like a candle flame burning undisturbed in a place without wind, a mastered mind stays steady and bright. Inner stillness protects you from the turbulent winds of everyday life.

siva_et: 6.20 When the mind, restrained by the practice of Yoga attains to quietude and when seeing the Self by the self, he is satisfied in his own Self.
summary: When you quiet your mind and look inward, you'll discover a deep, lasting contentment that comes entirely from your true self.

siva_et: 6.21 When he (the Yogi) feels that Infinite Bliss which can be grasped by the (pure) intellect and which transcends the senses, and established wherein he never moves from the Reality.
summary: There is a profound, limitless joy that goes far beyond what your senses can experience, and once you find it, you'll never lose your footing.

siva_et: 6.22 Which, having obtained, he thinks there is no other gain superior to it; wherein estabished, he is not moved even by heavy sorrow.
summary: Once you discover this inner treasure, no external prize will ever compare, and even the heaviest sorrows won't be able to shake you.

siva_et: 6.23 Let that be known by the name of Yoga, the severance from union with pain. This Yoga should be practised with determination and with an undesponding mind.
summary: True yoga is about completely cutting ties with pain. Keep practicing with a steady, hopeful heart, even when things get tough.
